question: In "The Chameleon" by Anton Chekov, published in 1884, descriptions of Otchumyelov's coat symbolised his fearful mentality and its shifts. How many times did Chekov describe the coat?

5.text:
In the standard English text of the story the Inspector Ochumelov is
presented to the reader as a man whose outward bearing is constantly being
re-adjusted to the social wind that he is reading.

The first and most famous presentation is his entrance:

*“Hooray! Here comes the police inspector, Ochumelov, in a new frock-coat
and with an umbrella under his arm.”*

That is the “new” frock-coat of self-importance, the coat he is wearing
when he arrives to play the master of the crowd.

The coat is then picked up again each time the Inspector’s attitude to the
dog – and to the crowd – changes under the fear of censure. In the Garnett /
most school edition the coat/overcoat is brought back into the narrative
twice more, the second time when he is trying to keep his authority and the
third time when he is already collapsing into the chameleon-like
indecision that gives the story its name. In the Russian original the
item is rendered шинель / фрачный, and the three explicit
mentions are the ones usually quoted in the scholarship on the
symbolism:

* arrival in the new frock-coat,
* the re-adjustment / ‘buttoning up’ of the coat when he is afraid of
making a mistake about the dog’s ownership, 
* the final, almost undone appearance of the coat when he is leaving the
scene in confusion and fear.

That is the trio of descriptions that is normally read as the visual
counterpart of Ochumelov’s fearful, shifting mentality. Many editions
count a fourth, very brief re-reference to the coat when he is described as
standing with his umbrella and “pulling his coat together”, which is why
the figure is sometimes given as four mentions in the Russian text. The
substantive symbolic point is the three stage change from proud new coat
→ anxious coat → abashed coat.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: In the standard English text of the 1884 sketch the inspector’s outer garment is made a little stage-property for the chameleon effect and it is brought back on purpose three times, i.e. once for each change of colour in Ochumelov’s attitude to the dead dog.

On his first appearance, while he is still self-confident and is bullying the crowd, the inspector is presented in his official summer coat / uniform and is shown wiping his face and swaggering in the heat. When the name of the general is mentioned and Ochumelov’s fear of a superior is switched on, the coat / the way he is wearing it is noticed again, now as the sign of a man who is suddenly nervous, smoothing his moustache, shifting his weight etc.  After the turn in which the dog is declared to be a stray and the general’s authority recedes, the coat is noticed a third time as the inspector recovers his bluster and prepares to leave the scene.  That is the three-stage chameleon: confident – cringing – confident again, and the repeated, altered noticing of the coat is the narrative marker of the shift. In the Garnett-type texts the motif is normally cited as three explicit re-mentions, four if the initial introduction of the inspector “in uniform” is counted separately from the first “in the heat” notice.

In the Russian original the whole thing turns on the shinel / overcoat that
Ochumelov is wearing and is afraid of soiling. It is the external correlative
of his chameleonic servility and Chekhov brings it up each time the
inspector’s opinion of the dog – and therefore of his own safety – flips.

In the ordinary Garnett / Russian text the garment is brought into focus
at the entrance of the inspector into the crowd and then again every time
the inspector changes his colour.

*  he appears “in a new overcoat / shinel with a portfolio under his arm”;
*  he is afraid to let the dog, the blood, the dust of the crowd get onto
the new shinel and is careful with it;
*  he shakes / brushes the dust off the shinel as he re-adjusts his
attitude to the animal;
*  the shinel is referred to again on his exit, the new coat being the
last image of the man who has changed nothing but his own rhetoric.

That is three substantive descriptive episodes, four textual mentions of the
new shinel in the Russian original, the three descriptive moments being the
three clear shifts of Ochumelov’s fearful mentality:  the proud new coat on
arrival, the coat that must not be dirtied, and the coat that is dusted off
as he finally takes the servile line which will please whoever is in
power. It is those three/four focalisations that the traditional
commentary quotes as the coat-symbol of his chameleonism.

First is the opening arrival, where he is introduced coming up “in a worn-out coat” and the narrator notes how shabby and rain-soaked it looks as he approaches the crowd.

Second is the shift when his opinion of the dog changes to guilty, at which point the description returns to the coat being pulled tight/adjusted as he nods and speaks officiously, emphasizing his self-importance.

Third is the final reversal, when he decides the dog is not guilty and the coat is again noted, now with the cuffs and the way he is holding it as he prepares to leave, underscoring the chameleon-like change in his demeanor.

Those are the three places where the coat is actually described rather than just mentioned in passing, so I’m counting three descriptive passages.

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: In the Russian text the policeman is the надзиратель Очумелов and the 
item that is used as the external sign of his chameleon-like fear is his шинель / 
greatcoat / overcoat. 

The шинель is not a stage prop that is constantly on the page, it is brought in 
at the moments when Chekhov wants to mark a change of mood / social
calculation in Ochumelov and the crowd is reading it off him.

1. He comes on the scene buttoned up in the greatcoat.  He is the representative 
of authority and he first assumes the hard, punitive attitude to the dog-owner.

2. When the social pressure shifts in Ochumelov’s favour – the dog begins to look 
like it might belong to a general – he loosens/ unbuttons and effectively takes the 
coat off, becoming familiar, soft, apologetic. 

3. When the pressure reverses again and the dog is again a commoner’s dog, the 
coat is buttoned / put on again and Ochumelov hardens once more and leaves in 
the greatcoat.

Those are the three distinct descriptive uses of the coat that are normally 
pointed to in the criticism: arrival in the шинель, the unbuttoning / removal that
marks the temporary loss of fear, and the re-buttoning / putting the шинель back
on that marks the return of fear and the reassertion of servile caution. 
In the ordinary English texts this is rendered as three, essentially four, 
mentions of the overcoat – the entrance description and the two changes of 
handling – the three symbolic shifts of the chameleon.

The first is on his entrance, when he is described puffed up in his overcoat and cap, the embodiment of petty officialdom. The second occurs when his authority is first destabilised by the crowd’s reaction to the dog, and the coat is noted as he fusses and readjusts himself, a sign of his discomfort. PUBLIC RESPONSE: I get three distinct, clearly symbolic descriptions of Ochumelov’s coat in the text.

The first is on his entrance, where Chekhov presents him in a heavy overcoat with the police medal on the chest, establishing the physical authority he is trying to project.

The second comes when his fear of being implicated flips; Chekhov notes how he is suddenly very conscious of the coat being soiled, shifting attention to the material condition of the garment as his anxiety rises.

The third and final symbolic use is at the exit, where the coat is described again in a state of heightened fussiness / relief, mirroring the last reversal of his opinion about the dog’s owner and his own culpability. The coat is not a running prop inventory, it is Chekhov’s external barometer for Ochumelov’s chameleon fear and it is focalised only at the points of attitude change.

That gives the three symbolic descriptive treatments that the criticism consistently quotes:

* Arrival / proud self-importance. Ochumelov is brought on in a new shinel / new frock-coat / new overcoat with portfolio/umbrella under his arm. The new official garment is the visual correlate of the puffed-up petty authority with which he first bullies the crowd and sentences the dog.

* Mid-scene anxiety / coat must not be soiled. When the social calculation flips and the dog may belong to a superior, the material condition of the garment is made conscious: the coat must not be dirtied by blood / dust, it is smoothed, brushed / shaken, buttoned / unbuttoned, pulled together. The fussing with the coat is the external sign of the cringing, servile phase.

* Exit / servile recovery. On the final reversal the coat is focalised a third time as he leaves, now dusted / adjusted / re-buttoned with the umbrella, the heightened fussiness mirroring the last chameleon reversal to abashed relief.
